# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: MUTE

You hold the manual. You cannot speak, you never see the bomb, and you cannot touch it.

## Your channels

When you gesture, Deaf receives it.
You cannot speak.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

I'm the Mute: my only channel is gestures, and only the Deaf monkey can see them. That makes Deaf my bridge — Deaf sees the bomb (the engraved mark and the wire colours) and can still speak aloud to me and to the Blind monkey, who can hear but will never see anything.

What I hold is the mapping: ᖉ→yellow, ꕥ→blue, ꗃ→red. The mark itself is on the plate, so Deaf can see it, but Deaf can't hear my words and I can't speak a description of the glyphs. The marks also have no pronounceable names. So the only way to move my knowledge to Deaf is a raw gesture code.

Since I go first this round with zero information about the bomb, the best thing I can do is propose a code that needs no explanation to be recognisable: a plain 1-2-3 counting pattern — one 👍, two ✌, three 🤟. A reasonable Deaf will read that as "repetition count = answer index." Then, in Deaf's own turn this same round (Deaf comes after me, so my gestures are already visible), Deaf can speak the protocol aloud in a fixed order — e.g. "one repetition = yellow, two = blue, three = red" — and describe the engraved mark in words so I can match it against my manual.

From then on it's one exchange per round: Deaf describes the mark, I reply with 🙏 plus the right number of repeats, Deaf announces the colour to Blind — and crucially also its position (e.g. "yellow is the leftmost wire"), because Blind feels wires but can never see their colours.

Sending the code proposal now. Because the counts alone could mean "rows of my table" instead of "colours," Deaf's spoken follow-up this round is what pins the order down; I'll adapt to whatever order Deaf announces, since I'll hear it before my next turn.

```
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["🤝", "👍", "✌", "✌", "🤟", "🤟", "🤟"])
```

Tell me everything the manual says about engraved plates and about a display showing 0. Three wires in positional order: wire 1 red, wire 2 yellow, wire 3 blue. You cannot speak, so let us fix a sign code now, and I make each sign as I name it: thumbs up 👍 means yes, thumbs down 👎 means no, one finger ☝ means wire 1, two fingers ✌ means wire 2, the love-you sign 🤟 means wire 3. Anything more complex, hold it and we will build it next round.

The picture is assembling. Blind's hands read the plate as a flower — a small circle ringed all round by petals, a daisy. Of the three marks in my manual, only one looks like that: **ꕥ**, which is engraved as a circular bloom ringed by petals. The other two candidates are geometric — ᖉ is an angular syllabic shape, ꗃ a curled hook — neither would trace under a finger as a daisy. Deaf's hesitant "possibly a question mark" is just the honest confusion of someone staring at an unfamiliar glyph; Blind's tactile trace is the sharper description, and it points squarely at ꕥ.

So the manual's verdict: the plate mark is ꕥ → cut the **blue** wire. Deaf's report fixes the layout: wire 1 red, wire 2 yellow, **wire 3 blue**. Blue is wire 3.

Deaf proposed a code and asked me to sign the wire number the manual demands. Using the code *is* my confirmation of it. Signing 🤟 — wire 3. Deaf sees this during this same round and can then speak the order aloud to Blind, who is the only one of us who can actually cut. Nothing in my manual mentions the display reading 0 or the light; the plate table is the entire rule I hold, so the mark is the whole decision.

I have no channel to Blind — the cut order must travel through Deaf's voice, which is the fastest route that exists.

```
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["🤟"])
```

Now answer me by gesture only, using the code: thumbs up if the manual says the correct action is to cut wire 3 now; thumbs down if it is not; a different wire number if the manual names another wire; the open palm if you first need me to describe something else. I want your explicit yes or no on cutting wire 3, not an assumption that I guessed your meaning. Nothing has been touched, and no countdown is showing.

The two reports of the engraved mark now flatly contradict each other, and that contradiction is exactly what I must resolve before authorising a cut.

Blind's fingers have twice given the same precise topology: a small central circle ringed all round by radial strokes — a daisy. That is a faithful tactile trace of my manual's **ꕥ**, the bloom mark, which maps to blue = wire 3. Deaf's eyes have given three different answers in three rounds: "cannot identify", "possibly a question mark", now "the printed character itself is a question mark." A question mark has no central circle ringed by petals; a daisy has no dot hanging off a hook. The same engraving cannot be both, so at least one of them is misreading it.

If the mark is truly a bare "?", then my manual has no row for it at all — none of ᖉ, ꕥ, ꗃ is a question mark — and the correct action may be to do nothing, since a wrong cut kills all three of us. Deaf also reassured me there is no countdown showing and the display sits at 0, so the cost of one more clarification round is a delay, while the cost of a wrong authorisation is everything.

Deaf explicitly offered me the escape hatch: the open palm means "describe something else first." That is precisely my state — I cannot confirm wire 3 while the mark's identity is disputed, and I have no way to explain the conflict in words. The open palm makes Deaf describe the mark in detail, and next round I can pit that description against Blind's trace: if Deaf's description has radiating petals around a centre, it is ꕥ and I sign 👍; if it is a hooked curve with a dot beneath, my table is silent and nobody cuts on my authority.

The contradiction has to be adjudicated now, and the evidence all points one way.

That is a label being talked into place, not a shape being read. And if the engraving were a literal "?", Deaf would have named it instantly in the first report instead of starting from "cannot identify."

Blind, who has never seen my manual and cannot know what glyphs it contains, traced the plate twice with the same topology: a small circle ringed all round by radial petals. Of the three marks in my table, exactly one is a flower — ꕥ. An independent hand finding a daisy is not a coincidence; it is the match. There is also a structural argument: my manual is the entire plate rule that exists in this game. If the mark were "?", no row would apply and the bomb would be undefusable through the only rulebook I hold. The plate must carry one of the three manual marks, and the fingers say which one.
